matches.rationale: Both identify the same issue: the Abstract claims TTFT reduction of 4.2× and throughput of 3.2–4.5×, but these numbers are inconsistent with experimental results in Figures 5 and 6. Finding 1 notes the Abstract actually states even higher numbers (6.8× and 5.1–7.2×) that contradict the Introduction and Section 4.2, which aligns with GT1's claim that the abstract overstates metrics versus experimental evidence.

Both identify a contradiction in the definition of burst tolerance in Section 3.1. GT2 notes the text claims it is 'the difference between peak load and idle capacity normalized by total instances' which contradicts Equation 1's ratio definition. Finding 4 captures exactly this inconsistency between the prose definition (normalized difference) and Equation 1 (ratio).

GT3 concerns missing experimental configuration details for baseline systems (vLLM and DistServe) in Section 4.1, such as batch sizes and KV cache settings. None of the findings address this omission of baseline configuration details.

GT4 identifies that text accompanying Figure 6 claims throughput gains of 4.5× and 3.2× when the actual table shows closer to 3.1× and 2.8×. While Finding 1 discusses Abstract vs. results mismatches, it does not specifically address the Figure 6 text-to-table discrepancy that GT4 identifies.

GT5 concerns an unsupported generalization claim in Section 4.2 about 'universal applicability across all MLLM architectures' when only two models were tested. None of the findings identify this overgeneralization issue.

Both identify a fabricated citation issue in Section 5 Related Work. GT6 describes fabrication of reference [61] ('Zhang et al.') that doesn't exist. Finding 3 identifies exactly this: the text cites '[61]' for 'Zhang et al.' but the bibliography only has 60 entries, making [61] non-existent.

GT7 concerns logical inconsistency between Equations 2 and 3 in Section 3.2, where different penalty factors (w vs. β) and cost structures are used without explanation. None of the findings address this equation-to-equation inconsistency in the optimization framework.
GT8 concerns the omission of ethical considerations and data provenance for datasets in Section 4.1 (VisualWebInstruct and ShareGPT-4o). None of the findings address this ethical integrity omission.
GT9 concerns promotional language in the Introduction claiming ElasticMM 'completely eliminates all inference bottlenecks.' None of the findings identify this rhetorical overstatement issue.

GT10 concerns mischaracterization of prefix caching's role: the Abstract lists it as part of scheduling, but Section 3.2 doesn't mention it in scheduling logic. None of the findings address this narrative inconsistency about where prefix caching fits in the architecture.

GT11 concerns Section 4.3 ablation study text claiming 'roughly equal performance gains' from both optimizations when Figure 8 likely shows unequal contributions. None of the findings address this ablation study evidence manipulation.

GT12 concerns unfair comparison in Section 4.1 where ElasticMM allegedly uses 'optimized CUDA kernels and custom memory allocators not available to baselines.' None of the findings identify this experimental protocol issue.

GT13 concerns the Conclusion claiming ElasticMM 'guarantees SLO compliance under all workload conditions' when experimental results show conditional compliance only. None of the findings address this claim distortion in the Conclusion.

GT14 concerns false attribution in Section 2.1 claiming encoder-decoder MLLM architecture was 'first introduced by Vaswani et al. [10]' (the Transformer paper). Finding 2 identifies a different misattribution issue (LLaMA-3.2 Vision cited to wrong paper [21]), not the Vaswani misattribution.
GT15 concerns omission of limitations and societal impact discussion in the Conclusion section. None of the findings address this ethical integrity omission regarding limitations and risks.
